_about.what: The war at sea. Fleets are counts of ships by class. A fleet on patrol holds a sea: it fights enemy fleets there, guards convoys and stops enemy troopships. A fleet raiding hunts merchant ships and avoids battle. A fleet in port is safe and refits.
_about.classes: power is a ship's weight in a fleet action. tough scales how likely it is to be sunk when its fleet takes losses (lower is tougher). escort is its worth guarding a convoy, raid its worth hunting one.
_about.quality: How well a navy fights, ship for ship.
_about.air: Aircraft flying from a sea's coasts count toward holding it. weight turns air strength into fleet strength. A surface fleet at sea where the enemy's air outweighs its own by more than 'safe' loses ships to bombers every month: lossPer of the fleet for each point beyond that, up to maxLoss. A computer-run admiral keeps out of water where the margin is over 'avoid'.
_about.closed: A sea is closed to a nation's troopships and supply ships when the enemy's strength there (ships at sea plus aircraft) is at least 'min' and at least 'ratio' times its own.
_about.ready: A fleet in harbour regains 'port' of its fitness for sea each month. On patrol it wears down to 'floor' and no further, and a damaged fleet that stays out mends only slowly. A battle costs the loser 'lost' and the winner 'won'. A computer-run fleet that has gone in to refit comes out again at sortieAt.
_about.battle: A patrolling fleet offers battle when it is at least 'seek' times as strong as the enemy in its sea. Raiding surface ships are brought to action with chance catchRaider. A fleet outnumbered by evadeAt or more slips away to port with chance evade.
_about.watch: The coast watch's report (the grand campaign). When a nation's month closes with 'corps' or more of its field corps standing idle on a quay, shipping for as many, and an enemy's home coast within a landing's range over seas open to its troopships, that enemy's coast watch reports it: his staff mans its harbours and a player is warned. Only a corps that has not moved in the month can embark, so the report is always a month ahead of the landing. The same quay is reported again only after 'every' months.
_about.intercept: Troopships crossing a sea where enemy ships or aircraft are at work lose men: up to 'loss' of a corps when the enemy is unopposed. 'sea' is how hard a convoy is to find.
_about.landing: A corps landing on a defended coast fights at 'assault' strength; in the month war is declared the defenders are caught unready and it fights at 'surprise' strength and cannot be intercepted. range is how many seas a landing force can cross. Enemy fleets in harbour on those seas or the next ones put to sea against an invasion at 'sortie' of their strength. No landing can be made under a sky the enemy's fighters still hold, unless it is a surprise. Airborne troops (corps marked 'airborne' in the setup) need no ships and no open sea lane: once a month they can be flown from a friendly coast to an enemy one across a single sea, and fight there at 'airborne' strength, without heavy weapons. craft lists, as [from turn, nations, strength], who has purpose-built landing ships and the naval gunfire to cover a beach, and from when: their assaults fight at that strength instead of 'assault'.
_about.convoys: Routes that feed a nation by sea. The share of the cargo lost is raiders / (raiders + escorts x escortWorth + ocean); 'share' of the nation's production rides on the route, and 'tons' is the shipping sunk in a month if nothing got through. 'base' is a fortress astride the route: while an enemy of the route's owner holds it, its own submarines and aircraft hunt the convoys with strength 'raid', or 'starved' of that when it is cut off itself. What is sunk on the Libya route also lengthens the supply line of the armies in the desert: see desert.json.
_about.ore: Swedish iron ore reaches Germany across the Baltic when it is free of ice, and down the Norwegian coast from Narvik when it is not. If neither way is open, Germany loses 'share' of her production.
_about.fleets: The navies of 1 September 1939. base is the region of the home port (null for a base off the map, with 'home' naming the sea it opens on) and port its name. zone is the sea the fleet is stationed in and duty what it does there. 'from' brings a fleet into being later in the war. 'open' holds what the row says instead in the grand campaign: Force H is at home in Gibraltar with the Western Mediterranean as its beat, tied to it, as the historian has it (historian/italian-boats-b562.md, part 2: the western Mediterranean first, the near Atlantic only for dated events; ruling 233 rider b564). The history campaigns keep the row as it was.
_about.building: Ships that join a fleet every month over a span of turns.
_about.arrivals: Single ships that join a fleet in a given month: [turn, nation, fleet, ships, what the news calls them]. A count below none is ships leaving. A sixth entry, where there is one, dates the row by the history dial: 'stops' are the grand campaign's stops it is read at (never in a history campaign, and never for the player's own navy), and 'sunk' counts the ships that leave as lost. Force H's carriers at stops 1 and 2 (historian/italian-boats-b562.md, part 2): the Ark Royal, torpedoed by U-81 on 13-14 November 1941, is gone from turn 28 (December 1941); the Eagle joins from turn 31 (March 1942) and is sunk in the Pedestal convoy on 11 August 1942 (turn 36). From stop 3 the carrier goes only if play sinks it.
_about.beats: Where a navy's submarines sail, by beat (ruling 233 rider b564; the historian's rows, historian/italian-boats-b562.md). Each group is a fleet: a group that gives only a name is the fleet of that name the navy already has (Italy's Submarine Fleet at La Spezia is the western beat), and the others are rows of their own, formed in the grand campaign the first month they have boats, with a line of news. 'held' is a place the group sails from only while the nation or an ally holds it; while it does not, the group is left out and its boats go to the others. 'stations' are dated changes of its beat: [from turn, sea]. Italy ('ITA'): the rows are [turn, then one count for each group in order: Atlantic, West, Centre, East], on the game's scale of 100 boats in June 1940 and net of the record's losses and new boats. Each beat takes its row's share of the boats Italy's groups actually have that month, so the game's own losses are never counted twice; after the last row its shares hold. The rows: the Mediterranean at 30/40/30 from turn 10 (June 1940), 15/25/20 from 15, 15/30/20 from 24 (it holds in December 1941), 25/25/10 from 39 (sent west against Torch), 15/30/5 from 45; the Atlantic from Bordeaux 8 at turn 13 (September 1940), 18 at 14, 26 at 15, 24 at 19, 27 at 21 (the four Red Sea boats round the Cape), 14 at 24, 11 at 29, 9 at 41 and none from 47 (July 1943), its beat the North Atlantic to turn 18 and the Iberian Coast from 19. At stops 1 to 3 the rows are read by date. At stops 4 and 5 the staff shares the boats by need (ruling 236 rider b554): each group's beat is the sea within its reach where the enemy's shipping is thickest (the sea lanes and convoy routes through it that feed a nation at war with Italy), its dated beat where none is thicker, and the boats are shared in proportion to that shipping; with none on any beat, as at turn 10. Germany ('GER'): the U-boats in the Mediterranean, taken from the fleet 'from' up to as many as it has: rows [turn, West, East], 6 from turn 26 (October 1941, all east), 20 from 28 (east 15, west 5), half west after Torch from 39, 13 from 53 (January 1944, mostly west), none from 61 (September 1944). When a row is lower than what is in the Mediterranean the rest go back to the fleet: play's losses are its own and none is invented. At stops 1 and 2 by date; at stops 3 to 5 only while the record's 'cause' holds: from its turn, an army of a nation in 'by' fighting on the African shore of the Mediterranean ('ground': Libya, Egypt west of Suez, Tunisia and Algeria), at war with a nation that holds ground there.
